deep.reconstruction:
Context: Chapter 16 of the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792) proves that every prime divisor of p^2+2q^2, with gcd(p,q)=1, is itself of the form x^2+2y^2. The previous page sets up the tools. (i) Para. 577-581: if a prime P = a^2+2b^2 divides p^2+2q^2, then the quotient is again of the form x^2+2y^2 (para. 578 gives the explicit identity). (ii) Para. 582-584: if p^2+2q^2 is divisible by a number frak{A} not of the form x^2+2y^2, the cofactor cannot be a product of primes A, B, C, ... of the form. Otherwise dividing these out one at a time would leave frak{A} of the form. So the cofactor, if prime, is not of the form; if composite, it has a prime factor not of the form. (iii) Para. 585: hence the excluded prime factors of p^2+2q^2 number either zero or at least two.

Para. 586 (this page): Euler warns that this does not yet show the following: if one factor of p^2+2q^2 (even a composite one) is of the form x^2+2y^2, then the other is too. What remains is to exclude p^2+2q^2 = frak{A}frak{B}, A frak{A}frak{B}, AB frak{A}frak{B}, etc. In each such case, stripping off the good primes A, B by (i) would make frak{A}frak{B} itself of the form x^2+2y^2.

Para. 587 (this page): infinite descent.
- Suppose frak{A} (implicitly a prime not of the form x^2+2y^2) divides p^2+2q^2.
- Replace p, q by their least absolute residues mod frak{A}. Then |p|, |q| < frak{A}/2, and frak{A} still divides p^2+2q^2.
- Hence p^2+2q^2 < (1/4 + 2/4) frak{A}^2 = (3/4) frak{A}^2.
- So the quotient Q = (p^2+2q^2)/frak{A} satisfies Q < (3/4) frak{A}.
- By (ii), Q is either itself not of the form, or has a prime factor frak{B} not of the form. In both cases there is an excluded number frak{B} <= Q < frak{A} that also divides p^2+2q^2.
- Repeating gives a strictly decreasing sequence of excluded divisors of numbers of the shape p^2+2q^2. So there would have to be a least excluded number dividing some x^2+2y^2.
- That is impossible: the smallest excluded prime, 5, divides no x^2+2y^2 with gcd(x,y)=1.
- Conclusion: numbers p^2+2q^2 (gcd(p,q)=1) have no prime divisors that are not themselves of the form x^2+2y^2.

The marginal note on p. 74 draws the corollary: primes 8n+5 and 8n+7 never divide p^2+2q^2, so -2 is a quadratic non-residue for them.

Implicit steps supplied by me:
- After reduction mod frak{A}, p and q may acquire a common factor d. Since frak{A} is prime and does not divide both, d is prime to frak{A}, and one may divide by d^2.
- Q = 1 is impossible, since then frak{A} = p^2+2q^2 would be of the form.
errors: Strictly one should write |p|,|q| <= (frak{A}-1)/2 (least absolute residues). This gives p^2+2q^2 <= 3(frak{A}-1)^2/4 < 3 frak{A}^2/4, so the strict inequalities are fine for odd frak{A}.

Coprimality after reduction mod frak{A} is not addressed. The reduced p, q may share a factor d; it must be divided out (harmless since d is prime to frak{A}). The step from Q to its excluded factor frak{B} via para. 583-584 also tacitly uses the coprime version of the division lemma.
frak{A} must be taken prime (as in para. 585) for the descent to be clean. The text says only 'numerum frak{A} non formae xx+2yy'.

The descent conclusion is phrased loosely ('minimus talis numerus ... assignari posset ... quod cum fieri nequeat'). The base case (no excluded prime as small as 5 divides a coprime x^2+2y^2) is not explicitly checked.
The concern raised in para. 586 (one composite factor of the form forcing the other to be) is not resolved on this page. It is not needed for the final statement about prime divisors.

results.what: Every prime divisor of p^2+2q^2 with gcd(p,q)=1 is of the form x^2+2y^2 (hence 2 or a prime ≡1,3 mod 8), proved by infinite descent with the bound p^2+2q^2 < (3/4)A^2
results.modern_name: Euler's descent proof for primes represented by x^2+2y^2 (theory of the principal form of discriminant -8); -2 is a non-residue mod primes ≡5,7 (mod 8), part of the second supplement to quadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Stated by Fermat (1654); Euler gave descent arguments (cf. E256, 1761, and this Tractatus, c. 1750s, published 1849); complete proof usually credited to Lagrange (1773-75)

results.what: Observation that the descent leaves open whether p^2+2q^2 could equal a product of two or more excluded primes, so the argument must target prime divisors directly
results.modern_name: Gap analysis in descent proofs (Euler's 'divisibility step' vs 'descent step')
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (discussed in Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History; Edwards)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known descent argument for divisors of x^2+2y^2, from the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina. It was published in Opera Posthuma (1849) and Opera Omnia I.5, and is discussed by Weil and others. Nothing here goes beyond what is already attributed to Euler.

checkable.asserts: Product of two numbers of the form x^2+2y^2 is of that form (underlies para. 583).
If |p|,|q| < A/2 then p^2+2q^2 < (3/4)A^2, so the quotient is < (3/4)A.
Using least absolute residues for odd A gives the strict bound p^2+2q^2 < 3A^2/4.

checkable.sympy: all(not any((x**2+2*y**2) % P == 0 and gcd(x,y)==1 for x in range(P) for y in range(1,P)) for P in primerange(3,200) if P % 8 in (5,7))
checkable.asserts: Primes ≡5,7 mod 8 divide no x^2+2y^2 with gcd(x,y)=1 (the theorem's corollary, marginal note on p. 74).

checkable.sympy: all(any(x**2+2*y**2 == P for x in range(1,isqrt(P)+1) for y in range(1,isqrt(P)+1)) for P in primerange(3,500) if P % 8 in (1,3))
checkable.asserts: Primes ≡1,3 mod 8 are of the form x^2+2y^2, consistent with the theorem.

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(-2 % P, P) == -1 for P in primerange(3,500) if P % 8 in (5,7))
checkable.asserts: -2 is a quadratic non-residue modulo primes ≡5,7 mod 8.

transcription_corrections: The printed '-+-' throughout is the period typography for '+'; the transcription's '+' is correct.
In para. 587 the bounds read p < (1/2)frak{A}, q < (1/2)frak{A}, pp+2qq < (3/4)frak{A}frak{A} and quotient < (3/4)frak{A}, matching the image; no substantive transcription errors found.
